analysis.one_liner: Requires all US electricity to come from renewable sources by 2035 and sets national climate targets.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Energy to write rules so that 100% of electricity sold in the US comes from renewable sources by 2035, and set yearly energy-saving targets for electric and gas suppliers, which suppliers could meet through a trading system. It also would have directed the EPA to set annual greenhouse gas targets cutting US emissions at least 52% below 2005 levels by 2035 and to zero by 2050, with final regulations to enforce them. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee, and died there without any hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would benefit from the bill's goals: less air pollution and a slower rise in the extreme weather, wildfire, and health harms the bill's own findings catalog [S3]. Households could save money through mandated end-use energy efficiency improvements at customer facilities [S2, S3]. The renewable energy industry would gain a guaranteed market as the electricity mandate ramps toward 100% by 2035 [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, clean-air communities, renewable energy firms

how_it_helps.text: Sets a national renewable electricity standard requiring the share of US retail electricity generated from renewable sources to rise every year and reach 100% by 2035.

Requires electricity and natural gas suppliers to deliver cumulative end-use energy savings (11.25% cumulative electricity savings by 2030), which the bill's findings say can save consumers money, and lets suppliers meet the targets through a market-based trading system.

Directs the EPA to set annual greenhouse gas targets so US net emissions are at least 52% below 2005 levels by 2035 and zero by 2050, with binding final regulations within seven years, to limit warming to the levels scientists say avoid the worst climate damage.
Preserves stricter state climate and clean-energy laws, so states that act faster are not held back.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and electric utilities that burn fossil fuels would bear the cost of replacing or cleaning up generation to meet a 100% renewable mandate by 2035 and EPA emission-reduction rules; some of those compliance costs could reach consumers through energy prices, though the bill's efficiency targets are designed to offset them with savings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and fossil-fired utilities

drawbacks.text: The bill sets extremely ambitious deadlines — 100% renewable electricity by 2035, roughly a decade out — without building new transmission, storage, or permitting reform, so compliance costs for utilities could be large and could be passed to consumers as higher energy prices.

The mandate defines the target only by 2035, leaving the year-by-year ramp and the content of the EPA's implementing regulations to later rulemaking, so the actual burden on any household or business would depend entirely on regulations written years after enactment.
The bill had essentially no bipartisan backing — a single cosponsor — so even supporters would have had to acknowledge it had no realistic path to becoming law in a Republican-controlled House.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits — cleaner air, mandated consumer energy savings, and emission cuts aligned with what the bill's own findings describe as the scientific consensus — are large, but the cost side is real and uncertain: a 100% renewable electricity mandate by 2035 is a heavier lift than most states have attempted, and the bill leaves the hardest details to future regulations. Honest supporters would call it an ambitious benchmark bill rather than ready-to-enact law; and in practice the cost question never arrived, because the bill never advanced past committee referral.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee, and it stayed there until the Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the Climate Solutions Act of 2023 on September 14, 2023.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on September 14, 2023, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials.
Only one other member cosponsored the bill, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, never having received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and utilities that would have faced the 100% renewable mandate and EPA emission rules are better off, since they face no federal requirement. The bill's sponsors lose the opportunity to set those targets in law.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only advocate in Congress; it received no committee action.

for.name: One House Democrat cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Added their name in support — the bill's entire cosponsor list was one member.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — during the full two-year Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee calendar and floor schedule and never advanced the bill; it drew no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support; with Republicans controlling the House committee that received it, it never moved.

industries.note: The bill would require natural gas suppliers to deliver rising annual savings and would subject any source of greenhouse gas emissions to EPA reduction rules on the way to net zero by 2050. The industry avoided all of this when the bill died in committee.
A 100% renewable electricity requirement by 2035 would force coal- and gas-fired generators to replace or retire that capacity. Stopping the bill preserved the status quo.
The bill would have guaranteed a growing market for renewable generation as the federal standard ramped to 100% by 2035. It died before creating that market.
